The raw dot products are then divided by the square root of the query and key dimension, denoted as $d_k$, and a softmax function is applied to these scaled scores to generate the final attention weights [S1]. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ is necessary to prevent the dot products from becoming too large in magnitude when the dimensionality is high [S1]. This scaling ensures that the attention mechanism remains stable and efficient during training for larger values of $d_k$ [S1].

The Transformer adds a positional encoding vector to each input token’s embedding so that the model can use token order, since it contains no recurrence or convolution [S1].  
The encoding is built by applying sine and cosine functions of different frequencies to the position index: for even‑indexed dimensions PE(pos,2i)=sin(pos/10000^{2i/d_model}) and for odd‑indexed dimensions PE(pos,2i+1)=cos(pos/10000^{2i/d_model}) [S1].  
Each dimension corresponds to a sinusoid, with wavelengths forming a geometric progression from 2π up to 10000·2π, allowing any fixed offset k to be expressed as a linear function of the base encoding, which facilitates learning relative positions [S1].  
The authors experimented with learned positional embeddings and observed nearly identical translation performance, but chose sinusoids because they enable the model to extrapolate to longer sequences than seen during training [S1][S2].  
Thus, sinusoids provide a simple, fixed, and smoothly varying encoding that supports both relative position learning and extrapolation, while learned embeddings offer comparable accuracy but lack this extrapolation property [S1][S2].

Helium supplies strong reasoning and linguistic knowledge to the system by providing pre‑trained text tokens that are used as prefixes for semantic generation, thereby improving factuality and linguistic quality during dialogue [S1][S2]. By combining the two audio streams in a depth‑wise Transformer that supports streaming inference, Moshi can process incoming speech and generate outgoing speech in parallel, thereby enabling both sides to speak at the same time[S3]. This design is further supported by the Mimi neural audio codec, which jointly encodes semantic and acoustic information into a single tokeniser, making the streaming of both streams efficient and high‑quality[S3]. drafts.new_text: Inner Monologue is a method that generates text tokens as a prefix to audio tokens while remaining compatible with streaming inference, allowing the model to decide whether the upcoming content should be dictated by previously generated audio or by future text [S2]. By inserting a controllable delay between the text sequence \(W_t\) and the audio tokens \(A_{t,q}\), the model can be re‑oriented to perform either ASR or TTS: setting the audio ahead of the text lets the model predict text conditioned on prior audio (yielding streaming ASR with precise word‑level alignment), whereas setting the text ahead of the audio lets the model generate audio conditioned on future text (yielding streaming TTS) [S3]. This single delay hyper‑parameter can be switched during inference, requiring no changes to the loss, architecture, or training data, and is demonstrated in Section 5.7 of the paper, where the authors train a unified model that can perform both tasks by simply adjusting the delay between modalities [S1][S3].

drafts.new_text: H‑Net’s chunking boundaries are produced by a learnable routing module that scores every byte position for whether it should be a boundary, using only the local vector and the full contextual embedding of that position within the current sequence [S2]. The module is trained jointly with the rest of the model; gradients flow through a straight‑through estimator so the binary decisions can be optimized end‑to‑end without external supervision [S2]. Because the routing module has access to the entire contextual representation, the boundaries it draws are data‑dependent and content‑aware—e.g., the first stage often places boundaries near whitespace or the first character of a word, while later stages merge whole words or semantic groups such as “the backbone” [S3]. Perturbation experiments show that the learned boundaries still separate semantic units even when the usual delimiters are removed, confirming that the model relies on context rather than fixed byte rules [S3]. Thus, H‑Net decides where to cut the byte stream by dynamically predicting boundary indicators from the learned contextual embeddings, learning this decision jointly with the overall model objective [S2][S3].

The ratio loss is introduced to prevent trivial compression outcomes and to steer the model toward a desired compression ratio; it is inspired by load‑balancing ideas from Mixture‑of‑Experts models [S1]. The loss is defined as  

\[
L_{\text{ratio}}=\frac{N}{N-1}\Bigl((N-1)F\,G+(1-F)(1-G)\Bigr),
\]

where the three symbols mean:  

* **\(F\)** is the fraction of vectors that are actually selected (i.e., retained) during chunking.  
* **\(G\)** is the average probability that the routing module assigns to a boundary, reflecting how often the model chooses to split between vectors.  
* **\(N\)** is a hyper‑parameter that sets the target compression ratio; the model is encouraged to keep about \(_N^1\) of the input vectors.  

When the selected fraction \(F\) matches the average boundary probability \(G\) at the target ratio, the loss attains its minimum, guiding the network toward the specified compression level while still allowing content‑adaptive decisions [S1].

The Transformer adds a positional encoding vector to each token embedding, where the encoding has the same dimension \(d_{\text{model}}\) and is defined by sine and cosine functions of varying frequencies: for even indices \(2i\) it uses \(\sin(\text{pos}/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}})\) and for odd indices \(2i+1\) it uses \(\cos(\text{pos}/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}})\) so that each dimension corresponds to a sinusoid whose wavelength forms a geometric progression [S1].  
These sinusoidal encodings were chosen because a fixed offset \(k\) between positions can be expressed as a linear function of the original encodings, making it easy for the model to learn relative positions [S1].  
The authors also tried learned positional embeddings and found that performance was nearly the same as with sinusoids [S2].  
However, they preferred the sinusoidal version because it can generalize to sequence lengths longer than those seen during training, whereas learned embeddings are limited to the lengths they were trained on [S1][S2].

Its multi‑stream design, built on the Helium text LLM and the Mimi neural audio codec, allows the model to process the incoming user audio stream while concurrently generating its own output audio stream in real time [S3].  The Depth Transformer backbone supports streaming inference for both streams, enabling continuous, overlapping speech processing rather than sequential turn‑based interaction [S3].  Inner Monologue further integrates text and audio token generation, letting the system exploit text‑language knowledge while still operating as a pure speech‑to‑speech model, which reinforces the ability to handle simultaneous speaking and listening [S3].  By separating and hierarchically synchronizing these token streams, Moshi can manage overlapping utterances from both parties without explicit speaker‑turn modeling, achieving true full‑duplex dialogue [S2][S3].

drafts.new_text: Inner Monologue is a method in Moshi that generates text tokens as a prefix to audio tokens, enabling the model to decide whether to produce speech or transcription based on the relative delay between the two streams [S3]. By inserting a configurable delay between the text sequence (W_t) and the audio tokens (A_t,q), the language model can be made to let audio dictate the text (streaming ASR) or let text dictate the audio (streaming TTS) without changing the loss, architecture, or training data [S2][S1]. For streaming ASR, the text tokens are delayed (e.g., by 2 seconds) so the model listens to audio before generating text, and during inference the audio tokens are teacher‑forced while only text tokens are sampled, yielding word‑level alignments [S1][S2]. For streaming TTS, the audio tokens are delayed (e.g., by 2 seconds) giving the model look‑ahead on the text, and at inference the text tokens are teacher‑forced while only audio tokens are sampled, producing speech with low latency [S1][S2]. The same single hyper‑parameter for delay thus switches the system between a streaming ASR and a streaming TTS model, illustrating the flexibility of Inner Monologue [S1][S3].

During training the model discovers that spacelike bytes (e.g., whitespace) are strong semantic delimiters, so the single‑stage version places most cuts at those positions, mirroring the behavior of handcrafted SpaceByte tokenizers [S1].  In the two‑stage hierarchy, the first stage still favours spacelike bytes but also often cuts after the first few characters of a word, allowing the remaining characters to become highly predictable [S1]. The boundary indicators are then used by a down‑sampler to retain only the selected vectors, effectively compressing the byte stream according to the learned, data‑dependent segmentation [S3].

For streaming TTS the training uses a 2‑second delay of audio tokens, giving the model look‑ahead on text and teacher‑forcing the text tokens at inference time, so that speech is produced with low latency [S1]. For streaming ASR the training delays the text tokens by the same 2‑second amount, allowing the model to ingest audio before emitting text and then teacher‑forcing the audio tokens at inference [S1]. Changing only this single delay hyper‑parameter switches the same Moshi model between TTS and ASR without any architectural, loss‑function, or data changes [S2][S7]. Thus Inner Monologue provides a unified, delay‑controlled framework for deriving both streaming speech synthesis and streaming speech recognition from one model.

The ratio loss is introduced to prevent the model from collapsing to trivial solutions that either keep almost all vectors (defeating compression) or discard too much information (losing important content) by explicitly encouraging a target compression ratio [S3].  
In this loss, F represents the average fraction of selected vectors (e.g., boundary decisions) across the sequence, computed as the mean of the binary selection indicators bₜ over all timesteps t [S3].  
G denotes the average fraction of predicted probabilities pₜ for those selections, i.e., the mean of the routing probabilities across the sequence [S3].  
N is the total number of possible slots (or experts) that could be selected, appearing in the denominator that scales the desired compression proportion [(N−1)F G + (1−F)(1‑G)] [S3].  
When F and G are equal, the loss attains its minimum value of 1 (at F = G = 1/N), which encourages the model to balance its utilization and achieve the intended compression ratio [S5].  
If F and G deviate, the loss can drop below 1, but in practice the architecture pushes F ≈ G, so the ratio loss effectively guides the model toward the desired compression behavior [S5].

Moshi is full‑duplex because it does not rely on a single, turn‑based token stream; instead it models the user’s speech and the system’s speech as two parallel streams of semantic and acoustic tokens that are generated hierarchically in real time[S2][S3].

Thus Moshi’s dual‑stream token generation and hierarchical, time‑aligned processing give it the ability to handle both participants speaking at once with low latency[S3][S4].

In the loss formulation, F denotes the actual fraction of vectors the model keeps, G represents the intended (target) compression fraction, and N is the total number of vectors in the sequence [S3].

Combined with the autoregressive prediction loss, this mechanism enables the model to learn which vectors to retain based on semantic importance rather than a fixed pattern [S3].

Inner Monologue is a method that generates text tokens as a prefix to audio tokens within Moshi’s hierarchical multi‑stream language model, while remaining compatible with streaming inference[S2].  
By inserting a configurable delay between the text sequence and the audio token sequence, the model can be made to let either the audio dictate the text (for ASR) or the text dictate the audio (for TTS) without changing the loss, architecture, or training data[S3].  
For streaming ASR, the text tokens are delayed (e.g., by 2 s) so that the model listens to audio before emitting text, and during inference the audio tokens are teacher‑forced while the model predicts the delayed text tokens, yielding word‑level alignments[S1][S3].  
For streaming TTS, the audio tokens are delayed (e.g., by 2 s) so that the model receives text ahead of the audio and predicts the delayed audio tokens, while the ground‑truth text tokens are teacher‑forced at inference, enabling low‑latency speech synthesis[S1][S3].  
Both configurations use the same underlying model and only differ by the chosen delay hyper‑parameter, allowing a single system to switch between streaming ASR and streaming TTS[S1][S3].
